label: Top-scoring (6 of 6)
essay:
Every argument about automation eventually arrives at the same buried assumption: that the machine decides. It does not. A robotic arm does not choose the warehouse it arrives in, the shift it eliminates, or the executive who signs for it. People make those decisions, and they make them behind closed doors. For that reason, Perspective Three is right that the crucial question is who decides, though it understates how difficult that answer is to implement.

Perspective One treats automation as a natural force, comparing it to earlier waves of technology that ultimately produced better work. The historical claim is not wrong. The loom did not end employment, and the spreadsheet did not end accounting. But the comparison hides the timeline. When a textile mill closed in 1955, a worker might find another mill; the new jobs appeared in roughly the same places, on roughly the same schedule, for roughly the same people. That is no longer reliably true. When a distribution center automates its sorting floor, the jobs created are engineering positions in another state, requiring credentials the displaced sorter does not have and cannot obtain in the eighteen months before savings run out. Perspective One is describing a real long-run pattern while ignoring that people live in the short run.

Perspective Two takes that short run seriously, which is its strength, and then proposes a remedy that does not work. Slowing automation preserves particular jobs for a while, but it does so by making the firm less competitive, which usually means the jobs disappear later and all at once rather than gradually. A town that blocks the automated plant does not keep the old plant; it loses the plant entirely to a county that said yes. Perspective Two correctly identifies that work supplies structure and dignity, not merely income, but it defends that dignity with a strategy almost certain to fail.

This is why the question of authority matters more than the question of speed. If workers hold a formal seat when automation decisions are made, the argument changes shape. Instead of asking whether the sorting floor should be automated, the discussion becomes when, on what schedule, with what retraining paid for by the savings the machines produce, and with which tasks reassigned rather than eliminated. German manufacturers, where employee representatives sit on supervisory boards, have automated aggressively without the abrupt community collapses that followed similar transitions elsewhere. The machines still arrived. The difference was that the people affected were in the room while the terms were set.

The honest objection to my position is that shared decision-making is slow, and that a firm negotiating its automation schedule may be beaten by a competitor that simply installs the equipment. That is a genuine cost. But every alternative also has a cost, and the costs of the other two are paid entirely by the people with the least ability to absorb them. A slightly slower transition that leaves a workforce intact is a better trade than a fast one that leaves a town hollow.

Automation is not a wave breaking over us. It is a series of choices, and the only real reform is to widen the circle of people who get to make them.

graderComments.ideasAndAnalysis: The essay opens by identifying and challenging a hidden assumption shared by the other perspectives, which immediately establishes a sophisticated critical context rather than a summary. The thesis endorses Perspective Three while explicitly noting that it understates implementation difficulty, a genuinely qualified position. Each competing perspective is engaged on its strongest terms before being limited.
graderComments.developmentAndSupport: The distinction between the long-run pattern and short-run lived experience does real analytical work, and the 1955 mill comparison makes the timeline argument concrete rather than asserted. The German supervisory board example supplies specific evidence for the central claim. Most impressively, the fifth paragraph raises the strongest objection to the writer's own position and answers it by comparing who bears the cost.
graderComments.organization: The sequence builds an argument rather than listing paragraphs: assumption, first counterview, second counterview, positive case, self-objection, close. Transitions carry logic instead of order, as in the pivot 'This is why the question of authority matters more than the question of speed.' The closing line returns to the opening image of choice without merely repeating it.
graderComments.languageUse: Sentence structure varies deliberately, with short declaratives such as 'It does not.' used for emphasis against longer analytical sentences. Word choice is precise and controlled, notably 'hollow' and 'absorb.' Grammar, usage, and mechanics are essentially error free throughout.

label: Developing (3 of 6)
essay:
Automation is a big issue in todays world. Machines are taking over more and more jobs and people have different opinions about this. Some people think its good and some people think its bad. I think automation is mostly good but we should be careful about it.

Perspective One says that automation is good because machines do dangerous and boring work and things get cheaper. I agree with this. For example self checkout machines at the grocery store make it faster to buy things. Also robots in factories can lift heavy things that would hurt a persons back. Nobody really wants to do a job that is boring and repetitive all day long anyway. Technology has always changed jobs and people always found new ones so it will probably happen again this time too.

Perspective Two says that automation is bad because people lose their jobs. This is also true in some ways. If someone works at a factory for twenty years and then a robot takes their job, that would be very hard for them. They might not know how to do anything else. Retraining programs exist but they dont always work. So this is a real problem that we should think about.

Perspective Three says workers should get to decide about automation. I think this is an interesting idea. If workers had a say then maybe things would be more fair. But I also think that companies need to make decisions fast to stay in business, so this might slow things down too much.

Overall I think automation is going to happen no matter what people think about it. The technology is here and companies are going to use it because it saves them money. The best thing we can do is help people who lose their jobs. The government could pay for retraining or offer money while people look for new work. Schools could also teach students skills that machines cant do, like being creative or working with people.

In conclusion, automation has good things and bad things about it. It makes things cheaper and takes away dangerous jobs, but it also puts people out of work. I think we should let automation happen but also help the people it hurts. That way we get the benefits of technology without leaving anyone behind.

graderComments.ideasAndAnalysis: The essay states a position and stays with it, but the thesis 'mostly good but we should be careful' is broad enough to avoid real commitment. Each perspective is summarized accurately and then judged as partly true, so the response reports on the debate rather than analyzing it. The reason automation should still proceed despite the job losses described in paragraph three is never worked out.
graderComments.developmentAndSupport: Examples are relevant but stay at the level of general knowledge, such as self checkout and factory robots, and none is developed past a sentence. The hypothetical twenty year factory worker is the closest thing to concrete evidence, and it is asserted rather than explored. The retraining and creativity suggestions in paragraph five arrive without any reasoning about why they would work.
graderComments.organization: The structure is clear and easy to follow, with one paragraph per perspective, but it is a list rather than an argument, and the paragraphs could be reordered without loss. Transitions are minimal, mostly 'Also' and 'Overall.' The conclusion restates the introduction almost point for point rather than advancing the idea.
graderComments.languageUse: The writing is generally clear, but apostrophes are omitted repeatedly in 'todays,' 'its,' 'persons,' 'dont,' and 'cant.' Sentences run long and loosely joined, as in the final sentence of paragraph two. Vocabulary is serviceable but plain, with heavy reliance on 'things' and 'good' and 'bad.'

label: High-scoring (5 of 6)
essay:
A number is useful only when everyone agrees what it measures. A thermometer reading means something because we know precisely what heat is being recorded. A standardized test score is treated with the same confidence, but nobody can say exactly what it captures: preparation, aptitude, endurance, family income, or simply familiarity with the format. Because the measurement is real but partial, Perspective Three offers the soundest approach. Tests should continue, but as one signal among several rather than the summary of a student.

Perspective Two argues for eliminating tests entirely, and its criticisms are fair. Expensive tutoring does raise scores, which means the test partly measures what a family can afford. Test preparation does consume weeks that might have gone to labs or writing. Yet abolition assumes that whatever replaces the score will be fairer, and there is little reason to believe it. Admissions readers who cannot compare a score compare essays polished by paid consultants, extracurriculars that require expensive travel teams, and recommendation letters from counselors managing four hundred students each. Every one of those signals bends toward wealth at least as sharply as a test score does, and unlike a score, none of them can be audited. Removing the imperfect measure does not produce a perfect one; it produces measures whose bias is harder to see.

Perspective One is right about that danger and wrong about the remedy. It concludes that because a common yardstick is valuable, the test should stay central. But a yardstick that captures only part of what matters becomes misleading precisely when it is treated as central. A student who works thirty hours a week at a restaurant and still earns a mid-range score has demonstrated something the number cannot express. Under Perspective One, that context disappears; under Perspective Three, the score becomes one line in a fuller record.

The practical difference shows up in what schools do with their time. When a score is decisive, a school rationally reorganizes itself around it, since nothing else moves the outcome. When the score is one factor among portfolios, projects, and transcripts, preparation still matters but stops crowding out everything else. My own school moved from six weeks of test drilling to two after the state reduced the weight of the exam, and the recovered weeks went to a research project that taught more about analysis than any practice section did.

The strongest objection to my view is that colleges claiming to use scores as one factor among many may still weight them heavily in practice, making the middle position a comfortable fiction. That risk is real, and it argues for transparency about how scores are actually used, not for returning to either extreme.

Tests measure something real. They simply do not measure everything, and the harm in the current system comes less from the existence of the exam than from the weight we place on a number we cannot fully define.

graderComments.ideasAndAnalysis: The thermometer opening frames the issue precisely as a measurement problem, and the thesis takes a clear, defensible middle position rather than a vague compromise. The argument that removing a visible bias produces less visible ones is genuinely insightful. The analysis of Perspective One is slightly compressed compared with the treatment of Perspective Two.
graderComments.developmentAndSupport: The catalog of alternative signals, consultants, travel teams, and overloaded counselors, gives real substance to the central claim. The student working thirty hours makes the limits of a score concrete, and the personal example of six weeks of drilling reduced to two supplies specific evidence, though its outcome is asserted rather than examined. The counterargument about colleges quietly overweighting scores is acknowledged and answered briefly.
graderComments.organization: The essay progresses logically from framing to the stronger opposing view to the weaker one to practical consequences. Transitions are purposeful, particularly 'Perspective One is right about that danger and wrong about the remedy.' The fourth and fifth paragraphs are somewhat shorter than the argument they carry warrants.
graderComments.languageUse: Sentences are varied and generally controlled, with effective parallel structure in the list of admissions signals. Diction is precise, as in 'audited' and 'decisive.' A few sentences are longer than they need to be, but errors are rare and never interfere with meaning.

label: Weak (2 of 6)
essay:
Standardized testing is a topic that alot of people talk about. Some people like tests and some people dont like tests. In my opinion tests are bad and schools shouldnt use them so much.

The first reason is that tests are stressful. When you have a big test coming up you get really nervous and cant sleep. My friend was so stressed about a test that she got sick. Stress is bad for teenagers and school shouldnt make you feel that way. Alot of students feel this way not just my friend.

Another reason is that tests dont show what you know. You could be really smart and just be bad at tests. Or you could be bad at tests because your a slow reader. That doesnt mean your not smart. It just means you are not good at that kind of thing. Teachers know how good you are at stuff better than a test does because they see you every day.

Perspective Two says tests should be eliminated and I agree with this perspective. Perspective One says they should stay but I dont agree. Perspective Three says they should be smaller which is kind of like Perspective One but not as much.

Also tests cost money. You have to pay to take them and you have to pay for classes to get ready for them. That is not fair for people who dont have alot of money. Rich kids can pay for tutors and get better scores. So the test isnt really fair at all.

Also the tests are to long. You have to sit there for hours and hours doing questions. By the end your so tired that you cant even think straight anymore. How is that supposed to show what a student knows. It doesnt show anything except who can sit still the longest. My cousin took one and said it was the longest day of her life and she was exhausted after.

In conclusion tests are stressful and they dont show what you really know and they cost money. Schools should use other things instead like grades and projects. Then students would be alot happier and school would be better for everyone. That is why I think standardized tests are bad.

graderComments.ideasAndAnalysis: A position is stated, that tests are bad and should be reduced, but it is never developed beyond a list of complaints. Paragraph four names all three perspectives without analyzing any of them, and the description of Perspective Three as 'kind of like Perspective One but not as much' shows the perspective was not understood. No opposing argument is considered anywhere in the essay.
graderComments.developmentAndSupport: Support consists of one anecdote about a friend getting sick and a series of unexamined assertions. The claim that teachers judge ability better than tests is asserted and immediately dropped. The fairness point about tutoring is the most promising idea in the essay, but it appears late, gets three sentences, and is never connected to the earlier reasons.
graderComments.organization: The essay follows a mechanical reason-by-reason list, and the fairness and test-length paragraphs both arrive after the perspectives paragraph with no connection to either. Transitions are limited to 'The first reason,' 'Another reason,' and 'Also,' which is used to open two separate paragraphs. The conclusion restacks three of the four reasons in one sentence and drops the fourth entirely.
graderComments.languageUse: Errors repeat throughout and often distract: 'alot' appears four times, 'your' is used for 'you're' three times, 'to' appears where 'too' is meant, and apostrophes are missing from 'dont,' 'shouldnt,' 'cant,' and 'isnt.' A direct question ends with a period rather than a question mark. Sentences are short and monotonous in structure, and word choice stays vague, relying on 'stuff,' 'things,' 'bad,' and 'really.'

label: Adequate (4 of 6)
essay:
Almost every high school student carries a phone, and schools have to decide what to do about it. Some ban them completely, some allow them in lessons, and some argue that the real issue is how classes are taught. I believe that phones should be restricted during class time but not banned from the school entirely, because students need to learn to manage the devices they will use for the rest of their lives.

Perspective One argues for a full ban, and its central point is strong. Attention is limited, and a phone is designed to interrupt. When my history class started collecting phones in a bin at the door, discussions noticeably improved, because students were not glancing down every few minutes. The apps students use are built by companies that profit from time spent, so expecting teenagers to resist them by willpower alone is unrealistic. Adults struggle with the same problem in meetings.

However, a total ban goes further than the problem requires. Students use phones to check bus schedules, coordinate rides after practice, and contact family members during the day. A rule that removes the device from the entire school day treats a classroom problem as if it were a building-wide one. It also removes any chance for students to practice self-control, which is a skill they will need immediately after graduation, when no one collects their phone at the door.

Perspective Two claims phones should be welcomed as learning tools, and there is some truth here. In my biology class we used our phones to photograph specimens and look up classifications, which was faster than walking to the computer lab. But Perspective Two overstates its case. Most classroom phone use is not research; it is messaging and video. Saying that adults use phones for work does not prove that a fifteen-year-old will use one that way during a lecture.

Perspective Three suggests the real problem is boring teaching. Better lessons certainly reduce distraction, and a class with clear tasks holds attention better than one with idle time. Still, this view asks too much of teachers. Even an excellent lesson cannot compete with an app engineered by hundreds of designers to be as compelling as possible. Improving instruction helps, but it is not a complete solution by itself.

The most workable policy is a middle one. Phones stay out of reach during instruction, in a bin or a pocket, and become available at lunch and between classes. Teachers can allow them for a specific task when the lesson genuinely calls for it. This approach protects the attention that learning requires while still letting students practice managing a device they will carry for the rest of their lives.

graderComments.ideasAndAnalysis: The thesis is clear and holds a consistent middle position, and all three perspectives are addressed with a fair-minded reading of each. The analysis identifies real limits, such as the point that a classroom problem does not require a building-wide rule. The reasoning stays at a sensible but expected level and does not push past the obvious objections to reach a deeper insight.
graderComments.developmentAndSupport: The history class bin and the biology specimen photographs are usefully specific and clearly the writer's own, which strengthens paragraphs two and four. Other support is thinner: the claim that adults struggle in meetings and the point about app designers are both left as assertions. The final paragraph proposes a policy without examining what would happen when it fails.
graderComments.organization: The structure is clear and easy to follow, moving through the perspectives in order and closing with a synthesis. Transitions such as 'However' and 'Still' signal shifts reliably, though most are simple contrast markers rather than logical links. The final paragraph functions as a genuine conclusion rather than a restatement, which is a strength.
graderComments.languageUse: Sentences are grammatically sound with some variety in length and structure. Word choice is appropriate but rarely striking, and phrases such as 'there is some truth here' are a bit routine. The phrase 'for the rest of their lives' appears in both the introduction and conclusion, which reads as repetition rather than deliberate framing.

label: Top-scoring (6 of 6)
essay:
The debate over phones in school is usually framed as a contest between discipline and relevance, as though the only choice were to confiscate the device or to build lessons around it. Both framings share a mistaken premise: that a phone is a tool, neutral until someone picks it up. A hammer is a tool. A phone is a tool attached to an industry whose revenue depends on capturing the attention of the person holding it. Once that asymmetry is admitted, Perspective Three, which blames dull teaching for distraction, becomes not just incomplete but unfair, and a restricted-access policy becomes the honest response.

Perspective Three contains a genuine observation. Students do reach for phones during dead time, and a class with a clear task holds attention better than one that ends ten minutes early. Any teacher who has watched a room drift during a slow transition knows this. But the perspective converts a partial truth into a full explanation, and the conversion places an impossible burden on individual teachers. It asks a person with thirty students, six classes, and a shared planning period to out-design software refined by continuous experimentation on hundreds of millions of users. When those lessons inevitably fail to hold every student, the framework supplies a ready verdict: the teacher was boring. That is not analysis. It is blame assigned to the party with the least leverage.

Perspective Two makes a related error by treating adult usage as proof of student readiness. Adults do research and collaborate on phones, and students should eventually do the same. But the argument assumes that a skill is learned by unrestricted exposure, which is not how any other demanding skill is taught. We do not teach driving by handing a sixteen-year-old the keys and trusting that the highway will instruct her. We teach it in stages, with supervision, in low-stakes conditions first. Treating a phone as self-teaching is not respect for students; it is an abdication dressed as trust.

Perspective One is closest to right and still slightly wrong. It correctly identifies attention as the scarce resource and the device as engineered to consume it. Where it errs is in extending the restriction across the entire day, including lunch, passing periods, and study hall. Those unstructured moments are precisely where supervised practice can happen, and a policy that removes the device for eight hours produces students who are compliant inside the building and helpless outside it. My own school ran both versions in consecutive years. Under the full-day ban, phone use exploded the moment students crossed the parking lot. Under the instruction-only restriction, several teachers reported the opposite: students who had been reminded of the rule at the start of class largely regulated themselves by spring.

A fair objection is that the instruction-only rule demands constant enforcement from teachers, while a full ban settles the question once. That cost is real, and it explains why so many schools choose the blunter policy. But enforcing a boundary is itself instruction. A rule that is explained, applied consistently, and relaxed at predictable moments teaches something a locked pouch cannot: that attention is a resource a person can learn to direct.

The goal is not a quiet building. It is a student who can put the phone down when no one is asking.

graderComments.ideasAndAnalysis: The essay rejects the framing shared by the perspectives before choosing among them, arguing that a phone is not a neutral tool because of the industry attached to it, and that premise then governs every later judgment. The critique of Perspective Three is unusually sharp: it grants the observation, then shows that the view assigns blame to the party with the least leverage. The thesis is precise about exactly where and when restriction applies.
graderComments.developmentAndSupport: The driver's education analogy does real argumentative work, showing why unrestricted exposure is not how demanding skills are taught. The two-year comparison at the writer's own school supplies evidence with a specific and unflattering detail, the surge in the parking lot, which makes it credible rather than convenient. The fifth paragraph raises the enforcement objection and turns it into support by reframing enforcement as instruction.
graderComments.organization: The perspectives are ordered by increasing correctness, from most flawed to closest to right, so the essay narrows toward its own position instead of listing views. The concession in paragraph two is placed before the critique, which makes the critique land harder. The two-sentence close is short by design and reframes the entire question rather than summarizing it.
graderComments.languageUse: Sentence lengths are varied with clear purpose, and the short judgments 'A hammer is a tool.' and 'That is not analysis.' land with force against the surrounding longer sentences. Diction is exact throughout, particularly 'asymmetry,' 'abdication,' and 'leverage.' The essay is free of grammatical and mechanical errors.
